name: Umar Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think, and they don't have to match. Can you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at an open-pit gold mine, about forty minutes up the valley road. The rig drills rows of holes in the bench, the holes get packed with explosives, and the next day that rock is gone. I've been there eighteen months, I came from driving forklifts in a supermarket warehouse, so I'm still learning to read the ground through the controls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the machine, honestly. I ask the AI on my phone about every fault code that comes up, and half the time I know what's wrong before the fitter does. What drains me is the money, I'm on the lowest band, and with Mei on a teaching assistant's wage and two kids we're broke by the twentieth of every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least the tools are useful, I use them every day for small stuff. I'd post something like, turns out it's a good calculator, not a new god. People at work would laugh, they already call me the robot guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine. The drills at our mine are already going semi-automatic, the newer rigs can drill a whole pattern by themselves while you watch. So hype or not, I want to be the person watching, not the person replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking to get on the newer autonomous rig, which I've done twice already. I'd do the free online course the manufacturer runs, at night after the kids are down. And I'd keep pushing at the union meetings for the company to share the savings from automation with the crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Life goes on, and I'm already doing the things I'd want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want to be the person watching. What does that job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the new rig, the operator sets the pattern on a tablet, checks the hole depths, and only takes the sticks when something goes wrong. One guy on our crew, Paulo, runs two rigs at once from a pickup parked on the bench. I want to be Paulo in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being junior and being broke. They give the new rigs to the guys with ten years in, and I can't afford to pay for a course that costs real money. So I do the free stuff and keep my hand up.

S0.say: He'd say the AI tools are useful for small things, more like a good calculator than a revolution. Workmates already call him the robot guy.
S0.think: He thinks automation of the drills is happening anyway, regardless of AI hype. His aim is to be the operator who supervises the machines rather than the one replaced.
S0.do: Keeps asking to move to the newer autonomous rig and takes the manufacturer's free online course at night. Pushes at union meetings for automation savings to be shared with the crews.
S0.feel: Calm, because he's already doing what he'd want to do.
S0.quote: I want to be Paulo in two years.
S0.fieldNote: Umar is already moving towards automation and uses AI daily for fault codes, which is unusual for a junior operator. His barriers are seniority and money rather than attitude. He combines enthusiasm for the machines with a firm view that savings should reach workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, but only if workers get a share of it. Robots should mean shorter weeks and safer jobs, not just bigger dividends. I'd share stuff about the four-day week and automation taxes, I already do a bit of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm better placed than most on the crew because I'm not afraid of the screens. But I'm also junior with no savings, so if they cut forty drillers to ten, I need to be one of the ten, and that's not guaranteed. Being keen isn't the same as being chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get trained on the autonomous rigs in the first six months, and ask if I can shadow Paulo on my days off. I'd use AI to build myself a little study plan and practise the control software on the simulator in the training room. I'd also back the union's push for a retraining fund, because the older guys on my crew will need it more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly excited. Like the first day at a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the older guys. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerhard, who taught me to drill. He's fifty-eight, he won't touch a tablet, and he knows more about rock than anyone at that mine. If they push him out, they lose all that, and he loses everything because he's got nothing else lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And at home, what changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mei we might be on a tighter budget for a year while I do extra training. We'd drop the second phone plan and the kids' tablet games subscription. Sara would complain, Idris wouldn't notice.

S1.say: He'd call it a chance, but only if workers share in it through shorter weeks, safer jobs or automation taxes, and he'd share posts saying so.
S1.think: He thinks he's better placed than most because he's comfortable with screens. But as a junior worker with no savings, he knows that being keen doesn't guarantee he's chosen.
S1.do: Pushes to be trained on autonomous rigs within six months and shadows a senior operator on days off. Uses AI to plan his study and practises on the simulator, backs the union's retraining fund and trims small household costs.
S1.feel: Slightly uneasy but mostly excited, like the first day at a new job.
S1.quote: Being keen isn't the same as being chosen.
S1.fieldNote: Umar sees this picture as an opening and acts fast, but he's realistic that eagerness may not beat seniority. His worry turns outward to older colleagues like his mentor. His progressive views shape what he asks for: shared gains rather than slowing the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public plan immediately: a basic income or something like it, paid out of what these machines earn. You can't switch off half the economy in two years and tell people to retrain. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, all my learning doesn't matter much if the AI can also run the autonomous rigs from a city office. The thing I was betting on, being the guy who watches the machines, gets taken too. And I've got less than a month in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still try to get into whatever monitoring jobs are left, for as long as they last. I'd help set up a group at the mine to push for a payout and income support, I'm good at the online side of that. We'd cut everything to the bone, and Mei and I would talk to her parents about the kids staying with them if we had to sell the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the calm one, and I'd be the one losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your bet doesn't pay off. Is there anything in that picture that still works for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the fixing side, for a while, robots break and somebody has to swap parts in the dust. But two years isn't enough to learn to be a proper fitter. So I'd be competing with fitters who already have the ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sara and Idris?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the machines got clever faster than people got organised, and we're going to have to be clever too. Sara's ten, she'd ask if we're poor now. I'd say we're careful now, which is true.

S2.say: He'd demand an immediate public plan such as a basic income funded by what the machines earn. He'd organise people, not just post online.
S2.think: He thinks his whole strategy of becoming a machine supervisor fails if AI can run the rigs from a remote office. With less than a month saved, he has no buffer.
S2.do: Chases any monitoring jobs left for as long as they last and helps set up a mine group pushing for payouts and income support. Cuts spending to the bone and talks with Mei's parents about the children staying with them if they must sell.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and unusually sleepless for someone who sees himself as the calm one.
S2.quote: I'd tell them the machines got clever faster than people got organised, and we're going to have to be clever too.
S2.fieldNote: This picture breaks Umar's plan, which depended on human supervisors staying needed. His adaptability shows in quickly moving to organising, but money leaves him exposed. He still frames things in terms of shared gains rather than stopping technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can see it coming, so there's no excuse for being caught out this time. I'd push for the mine to set up a transition fund now, paid from the automation savings. And I'd be telling people on the crew to start learning, today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to get properly good at the autonomous rigs and maybe get a fitter's or electrician's ticket. It still ends with the robots doing most of it. But I'd be one of the last people in the pit, not one of the first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the autonomous rig in the first year and start a part-time electrical apprenticeship if the mine offered one. I'd use AI to help me study and to find any grants for adult apprentices. And we'd try to save something every fortnight, even forty, so we're not starting from zero when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but focused. I'd have a plan and a clock, which is better than just a clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years of that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Long days, honestly. Twelve-hour shift, then an hour of study on the bus, then help Idris with his reading. Mei would carry more at home, and I'd owe her for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be one of the last out. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe there's work keeping the fleet running, maybe there's a basic income by then. I'd rather be in the room arguing about that with a bit of money saved than outside it with nothing.

S3.say: He'd say there's no excuse for being caught out when it can be seen coming, and he'd push for a transition fund paid from automation savings while urging crewmates to start learning now.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to master the autonomous rigs and perhaps earn a fitter's or electrician's ticket. The robots still win, but he'd be among the last out.
S3.do: Moves onto the autonomous rig in the first year and starts a part-time electrical apprenticeship if offered. Uses AI to study and search for adult apprentice grants, and saves even forty a fortnight.
S3.feel: Anxious but focused, with a plan as well as a deadline.
S3.quote: I'd have a plan and a clock, which is better than just a clock.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Umar's energy back into a workable plan. He's honest that the cost falls partly on his partner at home. He doesn't claim to know what comes after and holds on to having some savings and a voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to build a fair system, so let's build one. Retraining, a fund from the profits, maybe a shorter working week as the machines take over. I'd be at the meetings and online, the same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I think I'm fine for most of it. I'd be running fleets of rigs from a screen, maybe training the next lot, and earning more than now. The big question is what comes after fifty-three, and nobody knows that, me included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lay it out in steps: autonomous rig in year one, electrical ticket by year four, then aim for a control room or maintenance planning job. I'd start a small regular saving for the kids' education. And I'd stay active in the union, because a decade of changes is a decade of deals to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a question mark at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the ten-year picture compare to the five-year one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a sprint, ten is a long run. With ten I can take the apprenticeship slowly and not wreck the family doing it. And Sara would be through school, so whatever happens, she's had a normal run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about shared gains. What would that look like in your town, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A slice of every tonne goes into a town fund. It pays for the training centre, keeps the bus running, tops up people who lose shifts. The mine's been here forty years, the town should own a piece of what comes next.

S4.say: He'd say a decade is enough to build a fair system with retraining, a profits fund and perhaps a shorter working week, and he'd keep pushing at meetings and online.
S4.think: He thinks he'd be fine for most of the decade, running fleets of rigs and earning more. What happens after age fifty-three is an open question he can't answer.
S4.do: Plans in steps: autonomous rig in year one, an electrical ticket by year four, then a control room or maintenance planning role. Starts small regular saving for the children's education and stays active in the union.
S4.feel: Mostly hopeful, with a question mark at the end.
S4.quote: Five years is a sprint, ten is a long run.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Umar sees a full career path through the change and his tone lightens. He still flags uncertainty about the end point. His concrete idea of a per-tonne town fund shows how his politics and his optimism fit together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away the very thing I'm betting on, and we've got no savings to buy time. What would help is a basic income that starts fast and is paid for by the companies that use the robots. Plus paid training, so people like me with no money can actually afford to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I like the robots. I do, I think they're amazing. I just want the people who've breathed the dust to get something out of them too.

headlineQuote: I just want the people who've breathed the dust to get something out of them too.
portrait: Umar Chen is a 43-year-old blast-hole drill operator at a large open-pit gold mine, eighteen months in after years driving warehouse forklifts. He uses AI every day for fault codes and study, and is eager to move onto the autonomous rigs. Money is his main limit: he and his partner Mei, a teaching assistant, are broke by the twentieth of each month. He stays calm in the slow pictures and is alarmed by the two-year AGI picture, which wipes out his plan to supervise machines. With more time he builds a stepwise plan and pushes for automation gains to be shared with workers and the town.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it removes the supervising role he's betting on and they have no savings to buy time.
whatWouldHelp: A fast basic income paid for by companies using robots, and paid training so people without money can afford to learn.
